title: What is an exception (Common Language Runtime failure signal)
hook: When something goes wrong in C#, the runtime raises an exception — a typed object that carries a message and a stack trace. JavaScript can throw a string; C# requires a real Exception type.

blocks.text: An **exception** is an object derived from `System.Exception`. You create one with `throw`, and the **Common Language Runtime (CLR)** walks back up the call stack until it finds a matching `catch` block or the thread ends. The object carries a human-readable **Message**, a **StackTrace** showing where the failure started, and optionally an **InnerException** when one failure wraps another. Exceptions are for *unexpected* problems — broken invariants, failed I/O, invalid arguments — not for ordinary "not found" results on a hot lookup path.

entries.plainDefinition: The base type for all failure objects in .NET. Every throw must use a type that inherits from Exception.
The .NET runtime that executes your compiled code, manages memory, and handles exception unwinding.
entries.example: When throw runs, the CLR searches stack frames for a compatible catch.

entries.plainDefinition: A text record of which methods were running when the exception was thrown. Essential for debugging.
The keyword that signals failure and transfers control to the nearest matching catch or kills the thread.

blocks.text: Typed exceptions let callers and workers decide what to recover from. A queue consumer can retry on a timeout but let a programming bug bubble up. Because C# enforces the type system at compile time, you never wonder whether the caught value is a string, a number, or a real error object — unlike JavaScript, where `catch (e)` is a guessing game.

blocks.title: Exceptions are not control flow
blocks.body: Do not use throw/catch inside a tight CSV import loop to signal "row skipped." Use return values, `TryGet` patterns, or nullable results for expected outcomes. Reserve exceptions for states you cannot continue from normally.

items.title: throw creates the object
items.body: Your code constructs an Exception-derived object and executes throw. The CLR records the current stack frame.

items.title: Stack walk begins
items.body: The runtime pops frames one by one, looking for a catch whose type matches the thrown object.

items.title: catch runs or thread dies
items.body: If a matching catch is found, its block runs. If nothing matches, the exception is unhandled and the thread — often the whole process — terminates.

items.title: finally still runs
items.body: Any finally blocks attached to try statements along the unwind path execute before control leaves that try scope — even when rethrowing.

snippet.explanation: Line 6: Message is the developer-facing text you passed to the constructor. Line 7: StackTrace shows the call path — preserve it; never reset with throw ex (next topics).

snippet.label: Try-pattern instead of throw for expected misses
snippet.explanation: Line 3: a cache miss is normal. Returning false avoids throwing on every lookup. Reserve throw for states that mean "something is broken."

catch (e) — TS uses unknown; runtime can be anything
StackTrace property on the exception object

Thread dies; host may terminate the process

blocks.title: Throwing strings like JavaScript
blocks.body: throw "not found" does not compile in C#. Translating Node habits directly leads to compile errors — which is the point. Always throw a typed Exception.

blocks.title: Using exceptions in hot loops
blocks.body: Throwing and catching inside a million-row CSV parse is slow and hides logic. Use return codes or Try-methods for expected branches.

interviewTakeaways: throw requires System.Exception (or derived) — not arbitrary values.
Unhandled exceptions unwind to the thread start; hosts may tear down the process.
Use TryGet / nullable returns for expected misses, not exceptions.
commonPitfalls: Translating JS habits: throwing strings or anonymous objects.
Using exceptions for control flow in a tight CSV import loop.

jsTsCorrelations.note: JavaScript lets you throw anything — a string, a number, a plain object. C# exceptions always derive from Exception, so catch clauses can rely on types.
TypeScript catch (e: unknown) is honest typing because throw is untyped at runtime. C# catch (ArgumentException ex) is exact and checked by the compiler.
